cycle_time.insight: Cycle time is quite variable: the middle of the distribution is 19 days, but the slow tail extends to 97.2 days and beyond, which means delivery predictability is uneven. The improving trend suggests the system has recently been getting faster, but the long tail and the much slower bug items imply the gains are not yet consistent across work types.
evidence: bugs average 66.8 days cycle time vs 29.6 days for Product Backlog Items
cycle_time.watch_out: Check whether the slow tail is concentrated in downstream stages or in blocked items, because that will determine whether the main issue is flow capacity or dependency management.

lead_time.insight: Stakeholders can probably plan around roughly a month for typical work, but the slower tail still reaches 65 days, so commitments need buffer for outliers. The gap between lead time and cycle time suggests a meaningful part of elapsed time happens before active work or outside the main execution stages, especially for bugs.
evidence: median lead time 27.3 days vs median cycle time 19.0 days
bugs median lead time 45.0 days vs 27.3 days for Product Backlog Items
lead_time.watch_out: Inspect where the extra waiting sits: before development starts, in review/release, or in blocked states.

throughput.insight: Delivery is not yet steady enough to rely on smooth week-to-week forecasting: 8 of 13 weeks had zero completions, then output surged late in the window. That pattern suggests batchy completion rather than continuous flow, with recent acceleration but still unstable release rhythm.
evidence: weekly completions jumped to 7 in 2026-08-03 after multiple zero-completion weeks
throughput.watch_out: Watch whether recent high-completion weeks are repeatable or just clearing a backlog bubble.

time_in_columns.insight: Work accumulates most in Ready for release, where items spend the longest average time, so the system appears to slow after development and review rather than before work starts. If that queue is reduced, cycle time should improve materially because it is the most delayed stage in the process.
evidence: Ready for release mean 143.6 hours, highest of all columns
QA also averages 115.6 hours and In Review 104.4 hours
time_in_columns.watch_out: Determine whether release gating, external dependency approval, or batching is holding items in the final stages.

flow_efficiency.insight: A median flow efficiency of 51.4% indicates about half of elapsed time is waiting rather than actively being worked. The spread up to 100% and the 7 items below 20% show that some work flows well, but a sizable minority is spending most of its life idle in queues.
flow_efficiency.watch_out: Look for the specific waiting stages that dominate low-efficiency items, especially downstream queues.

work_start_efficiency.insight: Once items are committed, they usually start reasonably quickly, with no item below 50% efficiency and an average pre-dev wait of 8.2 days. That suggests the main delay is less about getting work onto the board and more about what happens after work has already begun.
evidence: mean wait before dev 8.2 days with 0 items below 50%
work_start_efficiency.watch_out: Check whether items that do wait to start are linked to prioritisation churn or ready-state congestion.

wip.insight: Current WIP is concentrated enough to create multitasking overhead, especially in Ready for release, New/Ready for Dev, and External Review. With 19 items in progress, Little's Law implies that if throughput stays near 1 item/week, reducing WIP is likely the fastest path to shorter cycle times.
evidence: Ready for release holds 5 items; New/Ready for Dev/External Review each hold 3
wip.watch_out: Test whether lower WIP can be sustained without starving downstream stages or creating more stop-start work.

wip_over_time.insight: WIP has generally declined from a peak of 27 to 20 recently, which suggests active management rather than purely passive accumulation. But the rebound from 8-13 to 20 in the last few weeks shows the system is still sensitive to intake bursts and can refill quickly.
evidence: WIP fell from 27 on 2026-05-14 to 8 on 2026-07-16
wip_over_time.watch_out: See whether the latest rise is temporary or the start of another accumulation cycle.

wip_age_distribution.insight: Ageing work is substantial: 7 of 19 active items are over 30 days old, and the median active age is 21.9 days. That means the team is tolerating a meaningful amount of old work, which weakens confidence that starting work translates into finishing it promptly.
evidence: 7 items over 30 days old out of 19 WIP
wip_age_distribution.watch_out: Check whether old items share the same stage, blocker type, or ownership pattern.

wip_age_by_column.insight: The oldest active items are concentrated in Ready for QA and Ready for release, with In Development also showing a long tail. That points to a downstream ageing problem with some upstream spillover, and the wide gap between medians and p85s suggests a mix of routine flow and a few severe outliers.
evidence: Ready for release max 138.8 days and p85 138.8 days
In Development p85 61.9 days vs median 35.8 days
wip_age_by_column.watch_out: Look for specific items stuck behind approval, environment, or dependency waits in the late stages.

blockers.insight: Blocking is costly and persistent: 4 items are currently blocked, and blocking has already consumed 270 days in total. The concentration in New and In Development suggests the team is carrying dependency issues both before and during execution, not just at the end of delivery.
evidence: blocked items are concentrated in New (3) and In Development (1)
blockers.watch_out: Investigate whether blocked work is being actively triaged or simply left to age in place.

blocked_by_signal.insight: All blocked items are marked as hard Blocked, with none on Hold, so the impediments look categorical rather than a mix of softer waiting states. That suggests the team has a relatively sharp blocker signal, but also that blocked work may only be captured once it is already severe.
blocked_by_signal.watch_out: Confirm whether any waiting work should actually be marked Hold but is not being flagged.

blockers_by_column.insight: Blocking is concentrated in the pre-development flow, especially New, with some in In Development. That leans toward a demand-side or dependency-clarification problem more than a pure downstream delivery bottleneck, although the blocked item in development shows execution can also stall once started.
evidence: no blocked items are reported in review, QA, or release columns
blockers_by_column.watch_out: Check whether items are entering the board before prerequisites are ready or before dependency resolution is complete.

blocker_timeline.insight: Blocking is broadly persistent across the whole window rather than a one-off spike, and the trend is only slowly improving. The weekly count stays between 3 and 4 in most weeks, which suggests blocking is structural enough to deserve system-level attention.
evidence: blocked count appears every week across 13 weeks
blocker_timeline.watch_out: Identify whether the slight improvement is due to fewer new blocked items or faster unblock resolution.

days_lost_to_blockers.insight: Blocked time appears to dominate the life of the oldest blocked items: the longest cases have spent 177 days blocked. That indicates blocking is not just incidental delay; for some items it is effectively the main condition of the work.
evidence: currently blocked items include one item with 0.0 days blocked in In Development
total days lost to blocking is 270.0
days_lost_to_blockers.watch_out: Compare blocked duration against total age for each blocked item to see whether these are unresolved dependencies or abandoned work.

stale_work.insight: Backlog hygiene looks weak: 104 items have not been updated for over 30 days, with many sitting untouched in New for months. That creates planning risk because the team’s apparent backlog size likely overstates usable, ready work.
evidence: many stale items are in New
some items have 148.9 days since last update
stale_work.watch_out: Distinguish between intentionally parked backlog and genuinely neglected work, because the response differs.

net_flow.insight: The system is not yet sustainable in its current form: 60 items arrived versus 17 completed over the window, so work entered much faster than it left. The recent weeks improved, but the overall delivery risk remains upward pressure on queues and ageing.
evidence: several weeks had strongly negative net flow, including -9 on 2026-06-22
net_flow.watch_out: See whether the recent balance in early August can be maintained or whether arrivals will again outpace departures.

arrival_departure.insight: No single stage is clearly accumulating or draining on a simple arrival-vs-departure basis, which means the bottleneck is probably more about time spent waiting than about a gross imbalance at one stage. The more nuanced timing metrics still show serious delay, so balance alone is hiding queue depth and ageing.
arrival_departure.watch_out: Use ageing and time-in-column data to find where balanced inflow/outflow still hides slow movement.

bugs.insight: Bug delivery is better than it was, but bug work still makes up a large share of WIP and likely steals capacity from features. Three bug completions in the last few weeks suggest some recovery, yet the open bug count remains high enough to keep quality work material.
bugs.watch_out: Check whether bug handling is interrupting feature flow or being treated as a separate queue.

bug_intake.insight: Bug intake was volatile, with a clear spike in late July, which may reflect defect discovery after delivery events or a release exposing latent issues. Total bug creation still exceeds completions over the period, so quality debt may be building even though some bugs are being cleared.
evidence: bug completions total 6 across three weeks
bug_intake.watch_out: Compare bug spikes to releases, experiments, or incident reports to see what drove the late-July surge.

bug_pct.insight: Bugs take a disproportionate share of active work, which suggests quality work is consuming a large slice of capacity. If 42.1% of WIP is bugs, feature throughput is likely being constrained even before considering the additional delay bugs create downstream.
evidence: 23 open bugs out of 62 total bugs
bug work appears in multiple columns including New, Ready for release, and In Development
bug_pct.watch_out: Track whether bug share falls as throughput stabilises, because otherwise feature capacity may stay compressed.

bug_net_flow.insight: Bug flow is still net negative overall: creation outpaces completion in the window, even though completions improved late in the period. That means quality debt may be shrinking in bursts but is not yet consistently being burned down.
evidence: bug creations exceed bug completions overall
bug_net_flow.watch_out: Monitor whether bug resolution continues at the late-period pace or falls back behind intake.

bug_distribution.insight: Most open bugs are still in New, with a smaller but important amount in release and QA-related stages. That means bugs are piling up both before triage and near completion, raising the risk of delayed fixes and release friction.
evidence: Ready for release holds 3 open bugs
Ready for QA, External Review, Ready for Dev, and In Development each hold at least 1-2 open bugs
bug_distribution.watch_out: Check whether New is acting as an untriaged queue and whether late-stage bugs are waiting on verification or release windows.

cfd.insight: The cumulative flow picture shows the system expanding rather than staying smooth, with one notable band widening in External Review. That supports the idea that flow is not evenly distributed across stages and confirms a downstream slowdown rather than a stable pipeline.
evidence: arrival_rate_per_week 7.8 vs departure_rate_per_week 4.5 in the CFD window
External Review is the widening band
cfd.watch_out: Validate whether External Review is the true accumulation point or whether it is a symptom of upstream batching.

wip_level_distribution.insight: WIP limits do not appear to be the main control mechanism here: most columns spend relatively little time at or above their limits, but Ready for release and QA are notable exceptions. Ready for release is the clearest structural pressure point, while Ready for QA is often empty and likely not constraining flow.
evidence: Ready for release is at or above limit 28.6% of days and over limit 14.3%
QA is at or above limit 34.1% of days and over limit 11.0%
Ready for QA is empty 48.4% of days
wip_level_distribution.watch_out: Check whether the limits are aligned with actual capacity or whether release/QA policies are driving artificial queues.

diagnostic_findings.finding: The main constraint appears downstream, not at intake or start-of-work.
evidence: Ready for release has the highest mean time in column at 143.6 hours
QA averages 115.6 hours and In Review 104.4 hours
work-start efficiency is 70.7% with a mean pre-dev wait of 8.2 days
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: Work usually starts reasonably promptly, but then slows heavily in review, QA, and especially release. That suggests the dominant bottleneck is in the later delivery stages rather than in getting items into development.
plausible_explanations: release approval or deployment gating is slow
QA capacity is insufficient or intermittently available
review/approval queues are batching work
dependencies are being discovered late in the flow
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Review stage-by-stage handoff times, who owns release approval, and whether items are waiting for external sign-off or test environments.

diagnostic_findings.finding: Delivery is batchy and capacity is not yet matched to intake.
evidence: 8 of 13 throughput weeks had zero completions
arrivals 60 vs completions 17 in the net-flow window
WIP rose from 8 to 20 in the last four snapshots
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: The team is not operating as a smooth pull system; work arrives faster than it is leaving and completions happen in bursts. That combination increases queue growth and makes forecasts less reliable.
plausible_explanations: work is released in batches rather than continuously
downstream stages clear in waves after long waits
too much concurrent work is starting relative to finish capacity
operational events such as releases or sprint boundaries drive batching
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Look at release cadence, deploy calendar, and whether completions cluster around specific ceremony or approval dates.

diagnostic_findings.finding: The team is carrying too much work for the observed completion rate.
evidence: median cycle time is 19.0 days with p85 97.2 days
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: At roughly one completion per week, 19 active items implies substantial queueing and context switching for the amount of throughput produced. Cutting WIP should shorten cycle time if throughput remains similar.
plausible_explanations: too many items are started at once
work is being kept open while waiting for downstream steps
capacity is spread across too many small queues
priority changes are fragmenting focus
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Compare individual cycle times before and after lower-WIP periods and ask whether the team is routinely multitasking across several columns.

diagnostic_findings.finding: Old work is being tolerated in the system, especially in late-stage queues.
evidence: 7 of 19 active items are over 30 days old
Ready for QA has median age 90.9 days
Ready for release has max age 138.8 days
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: The system is allowing stale items to remain visible and active for long periods, which usually means planning is operating on inventory that is not actually progressing. That undermines forecasting and makes current WIP look healthier than it is.
plausible_explanations: items are stuck behind unresolved dependencies
there is no explicit ageing or expedite policy
work is being parked while newer items get attention
ownership of old items is unclear
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Inspect the oldest items with their owners and last meaningful state changes, and ask whether they are still actively intended for completion.

evidence: total days lost to blocking is 270.0
blocking appears in every week of the window and is usually 3-4 items
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: Blocked work is a recurring feature of the system rather than a rare event, so it likely reflects recurring dependency or readiness issues. Because blocked time is so large, it is materially contributing to slower flow.
plausible_explanations: external dependencies are not being managed early
work enters development before prerequisites are ready
blocked status is only applied after delays become severe
teams lack a formal unblock escalation path
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Break down blocked reasons by dependency type and review how long it takes to escalate and clear blocked items.

diagnostic_findings.finding: Quality work is consuming a large share of delivery capacity.
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: A substantial portion of active effort is tied up in defects, which reduces capacity available for feature work and can also contribute to downstream queues. The team may be paying a quality tax that is visible in both bug inventory and release delay.
plausible_explanations: recent releases introduced defects
test coverage or prevention is insufficient
bug triage is slow so defects accumulate
feature work and bug work are competing in the same capacity pool
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Compare bug inflow to release events and ask whether bug work is interrupting planned feature delivery or being ring-fenced.

diagnostic_findings.finding: Upstream backlog hygiene is poor, but it is not the main bottleneck today.
evidence: many stale items are in New
diagnostic_findings.interpretation: There is a large amount of untouched backlog, yet once items are selected they generally start quickly. That means backlog hygiene is a planning problem and a visibility problem, but the bigger delivery pain is still later in the flow.
plausible_explanations: backlog is not being regularly groomed
some stale items are intentionally dormant
prioritisation happens just-in-time rather than continuously
different queues have separate readiness standards
diagnostic_findings.what_would_confirm_this: Review backlog refinement practice and distinguish intentionally parked items from stale candidates that should be removed or re-triaged.

outlier_patterns.pattern: The slowest completed items are concentrated in bugs and show a long-tail distribution rather than one uniform class of delay.
items_or_periods_involved: completed items with cycle-time tail, especially bug work
evidence: bug mean cycle time 66.8 days vs 29.6 days for Product Backlog Items
outlier_patterns.possible_meaning: Bug work may be more dependent on verification, environment access, or release windows than normal product work.
outlier_patterns.recommended_follow_up: Extract the longest completed bugs and check whether they were blocked, repeatedly bounced between stages, or waiting on external validation.

outlier_patterns.pattern: A small number of current items are extreme ageing outliers in release and QA queues.
evidence: 1190683 is a Bug in Ready for release aged 138.8 days
1212553 is a Bug in Ready for QA aged 90.9 days
1224507 is a Product Backlog Item in Ready for QA aged 57.1 days
outlier_patterns.possible_meaning: Late-stage queues may contain items that are effectively stalled or waiting on external action rather than active work.
outlier_patterns.recommended_follow_up: Ask owners of the oldest release/QA items what is blocking progress and whether any should be re-scoped, expedited, or removed.

outlier_patterns.pattern: One current development item is blocked while another development item has long total age but very recent movement.
evidence: 1235570 is blocked in In Development with age 35.8 days
1225384 is in In Development with age 61.9 days but only 0.1 days in column
1244470 is a Bug in In Development aged 13.1 days
outlier_patterns.possible_meaning: Development contains both active work and stalled work, so the stage may be absorbing interruptions or waiting on prerequisites.
outlier_patterns.recommended_follow_up: Check whether development items are being started before dependencies are resolved and whether blocked work is being left in place too long.

outlier_patterns.pattern: The most persistent stale items are overwhelmingly parked in New with no recent update for months.
evidence: many New items have 148.9 days since last update
New is also the largest source of blocked items
outlier_patterns.possible_meaning: The backlog may contain a large dormant inventory that is not being actively curated, which distorts planning and masks true demand.
outlier_patterns.recommended_follow_up: Sample the oldest New items and ask whether they are still relevant, duplicate, or awaiting external decisions.

outlier_patterns.pattern: The late-July to early-August window shows a clear batch clear-out followed by a refill.
outlier_patterns.possible_meaning: The team may be releasing in batches tied to cadence or ceremony, then starting new work before the system fully drains.
outlier_patterns.recommended_follow_up: Compare these weeks to release dates, QA sign-off dates, and intake spikes to see whether the pattern is operationally driven.

outlier_patterns.pattern: Open bugs are concentrated in New, but there is also a small tail of late-stage bugs.
items_or_periods_involved: New bug queue and release/QA bug queue
evidence: Ready for release has 3 open bugs
Ready for QA has 1 open bug
outlier_patterns.possible_meaning: The team has both triage backlog and near-done defect backlog, which can slow both intake and closeout.
outlier_patterns.recommended_follow_up: Separate triage flow from fix flow and inspect whether bugs are being prioritised or just accumulating in the backlog.

executive_summary.headline: The team is moving work through the system, but the late stages are slowing it down and queues are still building faster than they clear.
executive_summary.narrative: Work usually gets started without much delay, but then it spends a long time waiting near the end. A lot of active items are old, and several are blocked or sitting in release and QA for a long time. Delivery comes in bursts instead of a steady rhythm, which makes planning harder and increases the chance that work piles up. Bugs are taking a large share of effort, so feature capacity is being squeezed. The encouraging sign is that recent weeks are faster than earlier ones, but the system is not yet consistently flowing.
executive_summary.primary_diagnosis: The system is constrained mainly by downstream queueing and release/verification friction, amplified by persistent blocking and a large bug load.
executive_summary.main_caveat: The data shows where delay and accumulation occur, but not the exact operational cause of each queue, blocker, or stale item.

investigate_next.decision_it_would_inform: Whether to tighten, redesign, or simplify limits.

recommendations.action: Reduce WIP in late-stage queues, especially Ready for release and QA.
recommendations.why: These stages show the longest waits and the clearest ageing, so lowering work-in-progress there should shorten cycle time and reduce multitasking.
recommendations.first_step: Set a temporary cap on items allowed into Ready for release and QA until the oldest items are cleared.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: time_in_columns for Ready for release and QA; cycle_time median/p85
recommendations.expected_effect: Shorter queues, faster completion of near-done work, and lower tail latency.

recommendations.action: Create a dedicated unblock-and-expedite routine for blocked items.
recommendations.why: Blocking is persistent and costly, so old blocked items need active management rather than passive waiting.
recommendations.first_step: Review every currently blocked item in one meeting, assign an owner, and set a next action date.
recommendations.expected_effect: Fewer blocked items and shorter blocked durations.

recommendations.action: Triage and prune stale backlog items.
recommendations.why: A large dormant backlog reduces planning clarity and hides what is truly ready to work on.
recommendations.first_step: Sample the oldest items in New and mark each as active, parked, duplicate, or obsolete.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: stale_work count; age of items in New
recommendations.expected_effect: Cleaner backlog, better prioritisation, and less noise in planning.

recommendations.action: Separate bug handling from feature flow with an explicit capacity policy.
recommendations.why: Bug work is consuming a large share of WIP and appears to be competing with feature delivery.
recommendations.first_step: Agree a weekly capacity reservation or buffer for bugs and track bug intake versus completion separately.
recommendations.expected_effect: More stable feature throughput and reduced quality debt.

recommendations.action: Shorten the time items spend waiting before release and QA by tightening handoff criteria.
recommendations.why: The downstream queues suggest work is arriving into late stages before it is truly ready.
recommendations.first_step: Define a clear entry checklist for QA and release readiness, then audit the next 10 items against it.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: median age in Ready for QA and Ready for release
recommendations.expected_effect: Less back-and-forth and fewer aged items in late stages.

recommendations.action: Move toward smaller, more frequent releases.
recommendations.why: Batchy completion and bursty throughput suggest the system is clearing work in waves instead of continuously.
recommendations.first_step: Pick one product slice and release it on a smaller cadence for the next month.
recommendations.expected_effect: Smoother delivery and more predictable forecasting.

recommendations.action: Use WIP and ageing review as a regular management signal.
recommendations.why: The data shows that old items are tolerated until they become severe, so visibility alone is not enough.
recommendations.first_step: Add a weekly review of items over 14 and 30 days old with explicit decisions to continue, unblock, or drop.
recommendations.expected_effect: Fewer ageing surprises and earlier intervention on stuck work.

data_quality_caveats: The analysis window is only 3 months, so longer-term seasonal or release-cycle effects may be hidden.
Some charts use small samples, especially cycle time (13 items), lead time (15 items), and work-start efficiency (11 items).
Several metrics are based on snapshots of current items rather than full lifecycle histories, so they show accumulation but not exact causes.
Blocked duration and age values indicate severity, but the data does not explain the underlying blocker reasons.
The stale-work list is very large and truncated in the source, so only the pattern, not every item, can be fully inspected here.
Bug metrics mix all bug items without distinguishing severity or customer impact.
Arrival/departure balance by column can look healthy even when ageing is high, so it should not be read as proof of smooth flow.
